title: High Places
lead: Bamot, 'high places,' were local open-air shrines, often on hills, with altars and sometimes standing stones and Asherah poles. Israel worshiped the LORD at them before the temple, but Kings judges them by Deuteronomy's demand for one chosen place, and the prophets condemn them as sites of idolatry.

sections.b: Samuel blessed a sacrifice at a high place (1 Samuel 9:12–14), and Solomon worshiped at the great high place of Gibeon before the temple was built (1 Kings 3:2–4). After the temple, Kings treats them as a fault: Solomon builds high places for foreign gods (1 Kings 11:7), Jeroboam makes "a house of high places" (1 Kings 12:31), Judah builds them "on every high hill" (1 Kings 14:23), and even good kings of Judah are faulted because "the high places were not taken away" (1 Kings 15:14; 1 Kings 22:43). Hezekiah removed them (2 Kings 18:4, 22), Manasseh rebuilt them (2 Kings 21:3), and Josiah destroyed them, from Bethel to the Mount of Olives (2 Kings 23:8, 13, 15). The rule behind the verdicts is Deuteronomy 12: sacrifice only at the place the LORD will choose. Archaeologists have found open-air shrines and small temples at Arad, Dan and elsewhere that show what such sites looked like.
